newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Angry Bulgarians set to shun ex-communists in poll.
newsitem.headline: Angry Bulgarians set to shun ex-communists in poll.

text.p: Bulgaria, scorned even by its Balkan neighbours as the reform laggard of eastern Europe, looked set to hand victory to anti-communist opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov in Sunday's presidential election.

Seven years after the bloodless overthrow of their communist regime, Bulgarians feel cheated of the fruits the changes were meant to bring and now face a winter of severe food and fuel shortages and possible hyperinflation.

Even workers in the smokestack industries of Bulgaria's red heartland were deserting the governing Socialists, unimpressed by their candidate Ivan Marazov's nostalgic reminiscences about the cheap bread and safe streets of communist times.
Bombings and other violence have marred Bulgaria's second post-communist presidential campaign, culminating in the murder last month of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
Shortly after Sunday's voting began, police scrambled to a city centre school where President Zhelyu Zhelev was due to cast his ballot after a caller telephoned a bomb threat.
A thorough search found nothing, state radio said.

Zhelev, a pro-market liberal like Stoyanov, has not stood for re-election this time round. Stoyanov won 43.9 percent in a first round of voting last weekend, comfortably ahead of Marazov but short of the 50 percent he needed to win outright.

"I will vote for Stoyanov. We have to get these communists off our backs. They have brought this place to ruin," Stoyan Petrov told Reuters near the grim Stalinesque steelworks where he works in the town of Pernik west of the capital Sofia.
"I have worked like a slave for 20 years and now I have to think twice before buying meat or milk or paying my bills."

Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution the president is a largely ceremonial figure and real power lies with parliament where Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) has a clear majority.
However a big win for Stoyanov could widen rifts in the BSP between its social democratic wing and hardline opponents of change and perhaps help trigger early parliamentary elections.
Opinion polls give lawyer Stoyanov between 57 and 64 percent of the vote this time, well ahead of Marazov, who is Culture Minister in Videnov's government.
Voting coincides with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for release of a delayed $115 million credit vital to stop Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.
The mission's head, Ann McGuirk, was due to meet Videnov later on Sunday. Failure to break the deadlock could spark financial meltdown, ministers have warned.
Stoyanov and his Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) accuse the government of moving too slowly to privatise the debt-ridden economy and close big state loss-makers.
Bulgaria has managed to privatise a mere five percent of state industry, with most of the cash going into the pockets of shadowy business groupings close to the BSP.

Neighbouring Romania and Yugoslavia, also voting on Sunday, are themselves battling economic crisis but Bulgaria has the lowest foreign investment in the region and a quarter of its numerous banks are in receivership.
As other ex-Warsaw Pact countries hurriedly queue to join the European Union and NATO, Bulgaria still looks wistfully towards Moscow, its historic patron and protector.
Marazov has said he will try to revive trade links with the former Soviet republics if elected.

In Bucharest President Ion Iliescu, echoing a theme of this year's Russian and Albanian election campaigns, has assured Romanian voters that supporting him will prevent a Bulgarian-style crisis in their country.
The respected financial weekly Kapital said Bulgaria had become the "shame of eastern Europe".
"Even banana republics like Ecuador and Panama have long been considered more reliable partners for investors than Bulgaria. If we can't even qualify as a banana state what can we do?"
